description: Belly breathing guide: slow diaphragm breaths that relax and gently lift the pelvic floor, how it should feel, mistakes, easier and harder versions.
intro: Belly breathing links the diaphragm, your main breathing muscle, with the pelvic floor. As you inhale, the pelvic floor softens and lowers a little; as you exhale, it rises. Learning to let it relax matters as much as learning to squeeze.
feel: On the inhale, the hand on your belly rises and the base of the pelvis feels like it widens and softens. On the exhale, the belly falls and you may notice a light lift inside. Shoulders, neck and jaw stay relaxed. Avoid chest-only breathing, forcing the belly out or straining.

mistakes.wrong: Breathing only into the upper chest
mistakes.right: Keep one hand on your belly and one on your chest. The lower hand should move more, with the ribs widening sideways.
Let the breath arrive on its own. Forcing it pushes down on the pelvic floor instead of letting it soften.

mistakes.wrong: Breathing too fast or too deep
mistakes.right: Keep a slow, comfortable pace. If you feel dizzy, take smaller breaths and rest.

easier: Lie on your back with knees bent and a pillow under your head, and do a few breaths at a time.
harder: Add a gentle Kegel on each exhale and a full release on each inhale. Practice sitting or standing too.
who: Everyone, especially people with a tense pelvic floor, pelvic pain or stress, and people after childbirth once cleared. Lifters can use it to learn breath control.
skip: This is gentle and suits most people. If you feel dizzy, short of breath or anxious, return to normal breathing, and talk to a doctor if a lung or heart condition affects your breathing. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: How does breathing affect the pelvic floor?
faq.a: The diaphragm and pelvic floor move together like a piston. Inhale and the pelvic floor lowers and relaxes; exhale and it rises.

faq.q: Can breathing help a tight pelvic floor?
faq.a: Slow belly breathing can help the muscles let go, often the first step for a pelvic floor that is too tight. Relax first rather than squeezing more, and see a pelvic floor physiotherapist if symptoms persist.
